a1.title: Flowers on the Old Train Line
a1.excerpt: An old train line is now a long path with flowers, bees and butterflies.
a1.body:
A small town has an old train line. Trains do not use it now.

Rosa is 71. She loves flowers. Every day, she puts seeds by the line. Her friends help her. Now 400 people help!

The path is 12 kilometres long. It has red, yellow and blue flowers. Butterflies and bees love the flowers. Children count the butterflies every Friday.

Children walk to school on the path. Adults ride bikes to work.

“I love this path,” says Rosa. “It is my happy place.”

a2.title: An Old Train Line Becomes a Flower Path
a2.excerpt: A retired train driver planted flowers by an old railway, and now the whole town walks there.
a2.body:
Trains stopped on the town's old line 20 years ago. After that, the tracks were full of rubbish and weeds.

Two years ago, Rosa, a retired train driver, had an idea. She started to plant wildflower seeds next to the old tracks. Her neighbours saw her and wanted to help. Now 400 volunteers work on the path.

Today the path is 12 kilometres long. It goes from the town centre to the next village. There are flowers in every colour. Butterflies and bees came back, too.

Children from the local school count the butterflies every Friday. This summer, they found 31 different kinds.

Many people now walk or cycle to work on the path. “I drove trains here for 30 years,” Rosa said. “Walking here is even better.”

b1.title: An Abandoned Railway Blooms Into a 12-Kilometre Flower Path
b1.excerpt: What started as one retired train driver throwing seeds on a dog walk has grown into a wildflower path that the whole town now uses every day.
b1.body:
For twenty years, the old railway line on the edge of town was a place people tried to avoid. The trains had stopped running, and the tracks slowly disappeared under rubbish and weeds.

Then, two years ago, Rosa Ellery, a 71-year-old retired train driver, decided to do something about it. While she was walking her dog along the line one spring morning, she began throwing wildflower seeds onto the empty ground. “I wasn't planning anything big,” she laughs. “I just wanted some colour.”

Her neighbours soon noticed. First a few of them joined in, then whole families. Today, around 400 volunteers look after a 12-kilometre path that runs from the town centre to the next village.

The results have surprised everyone. Butterflies and bees have returned in large numbers, and pupils from the local primary school count them every Friday. This summer they recorded 31 different species of butterfly — more than anyone in town can remember.

The path has also changed daily life. Many residents now walk or cycle to work instead of driving, and volunteers have turned the old station building into a small tea room.

“I drove trains on this line for thirty years,” Rosa says. “Walking it slowly is even better.”

A nearby town has already asked for advice. If its plan goes ahead, the flower path will be twice as long by next summer.

b2.title: How a Forgotten Railway Became a 12-Kilometre River of Wildflowers
b2.excerpt: Two years after a retired train driver began scattering seeds along a disused line, the town has a flower-lined route to work, a booming butterfly population and neighbours who want to copy the idea.
b2.body:
For the best part of two decades, the disused railway line that curls around the edge of town was considered an eyesore. Once the last train had been withdrawn, the tracks were gradually swallowed by weeds, broken fencing and the occasional abandoned sofa.

That began to change two years ago, when Rosa Ellery, a 71-year-old retired train driver, started scattering wildflower seeds along the line while walking her dog. “I didn't have a plan,” she admitted. “If someone had told me it would turn into all this, I would have laughed.”

Word spread quickly. A handful of neighbours joined her that first spring; by the following year, whole families were turning up at weekends with spades and wheelbarrows. The project is now run by around 400 volunteers, and the path they have created stretches for 12 kilometres, from the town centre to the neighbouring village.

The ecological effects have been striking. Butterflies and bees, which had been in steady decline locally, have returned in numbers that took even experienced naturalists by surprise. Pupils from the town's primary school carry out a butterfly count every Friday, and this summer they recorded 31 species — a figure their teacher described as “almost unbelievable”.

The path has also reshaped everyday routines. Many residents who live close to the route now walk or cycle to work, and the old station building, which had been boarded up for years, has been converted into a tea room staffed entirely by volunteers.

For Rosa, the story has come full circle. “I drove trains along this line for thirty years,” she said. “I never imagined I'd be happier walking it at a snail's pace.”

Not everyone was convinced at first. Some residents said they had worried that the path would attract litter rather than wildlife. “If you'd asked me two years ago, I'd have said it was a waste of time,” one former sceptic admitted. “I've never been so glad to be wrong.”

Officials from a nearby town have already visited to learn how the scheme works. If their plans are approved, the flower path could double in length by next summer.

c1.title: The Line That Bloomed: How a Retired Train Driver Rewilded a Town's Forgotten Railway
c1.excerpt: What began as one woman scattering seeds on her morning dog walk has become a 12-kilometre wildflower corridor, a commuter route and — to the quiet astonishment of local naturalists — a haven for 31 species of butterfly.
c1.body:
For almost twenty years, the disused railway line that loops around the southern edge of town occupied a peculiar place in the local imagination: too long to ignore, too neglected to love. Once the final service had been withdrawn, nature and neglect set to work in roughly equal measure, and the tracks vanished beneath brambles, rusting fencing and the occasional fly-tipped mattress.

Few would have predicted that its revival would begin with a single pocketful of seeds. Two years ago, Rosa Ellery, a 71-year-old retired train driver, began scattering wildflower mixes along the embankments during her morning walks with her dog. “There was no grand strategy,” she insists. “I'd spent three decades looking at that line through a windscreen. I suppose I simply wanted to see it in colour.”

Colour, as it turned out, proved infectious. Within weeks, a handful of neighbours had joined her; by the following spring, entire families were arriving at weekends armed with spades, wheelbarrows and flasks of tea. What had been an informal hobby acquired a committee, a mailing list and, eventually, a name — the Bloom Line — along with roughly 400 regular volunteers. Together they have cleared, seeded and signposted a continuous 12-kilometre path running from the town centre to the neighbouring village.

The ecological dividend has been remarkable. Pollinators that had been in steady local decline have returned in numbers that caught even seasoned naturalists off guard. Every Friday, pupils from the town's primary school conduct a butterfly survey along a fixed stretch of the route; this summer, they logged 31 distinct species. “When the children first reported that figure, I assumed they'd double-counted,” their teacher admits. “We checked. They hadn't.”

Nor has the transformation been confined to wildlife. The corridor has quietly rewired the town's daily rhythms. Growing numbers of residents living within walking distance of the path now commute on foot or by bicycle, while the derelict station building, boarded up for as long as most people can remember, has reopened as a volunteer-run tea room. Its walls are lined with old timetables, and its best-selling cake is, inevitably, a lemon sponge named after the line's last scheduled train.

The volunteers themselves are a strikingly mixed crowd. On a typical Saturday, retired engineers debate drainage with students from the local college, while toddlers are dispatched, with great ceremony, to scatter seed along freshly raked verges. Membership, Rosa notes approvingly, requires no expertise whatsoever: “If you can carry a watering can and put up with a little mud, you're in.”

Not everyone was persuaded from the outset. Early critics warned that an unlit path would attract litter rather than wildlife, and several questioned why public land should be handed over to what one councillor dismissed as “a gardening club with ambitions”. Many of those voices have since softened. “Had you asked me two years ago, I'd have called it a waste of effort,” says one former sceptic, now a regular on the Saturday weeding rota. “Rarely have I been so pleased to be proved wrong.”

For Rosa herself, the project has a symmetry she clearly relishes. “I drove this line for thirty years, always watching the clock,” she says. “Now I walk it at the pace of a bumblebee, and I've never enjoyed it more.”

The idea is already spreading. A delegation from a nearby town visited in August to study how the scheme is organised, and should their proposal secure approval, the flower corridor could double in length by next summer — linking two communities by something rather more fragrant than steel.
